name: Met Office
text: Your train passes near the headquarters of the Met Office, on the train's {side}. The national weather service moved here from Bracknell in 2003; it was founded in 1854 as a service to sailors.

name: Sandy Park
text: Your train passes near Sandy Park, on the train's {side}, home of the Exeter Chiefs rugby club since 2006, beside junction 30 of the M5.

name: Broadway House, Topsham
text: Your train passes near Broadway House in Topsham, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Georgian house of 1776. In the 1800s a naval officer who lived there opened it to the public as a museum of antiquities and fossils.

name: Bridge Inn, Topsham
text: Your train passes near the Bridge Inn at Topsham, on the train's {side}, a pub since at least 1797 on a site recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1998 Queen Elizabeth II paid what was reported as her first official visit to a pub there.

name: Commando Training Centre Royal Marines
text: Your train passes the Commando Training Centre Royal Marines, on the train's {side}, the main training centre of the Royal Marines. Lympstone Commando station, opened in 1976, is there to serve it.

name: Nutwell Court
text: Your train passes near Nutwell Court, on the train's {side}, a neo-classical house of about 1800 on the bank of the Exe estuary, almost facing Powderham Castle on the far side. It was built for a nephew of the last of the Drake baronets, who had lived in the older house here.

name: A la Ronde
text: Your train passes near the grounds of A la Ronde, on the train's {side}, a 16-sided house built for two cousins, Jane and Mary Parminter, who came home from a tour of Europe and set up house together in Devon in 1795. It now belongs to the National Trust.

name: Bargate
text: Your train passes near the Bargate, on the train's {side}, the main gateway through Southampton's medieval town walls, built in about 1180. It was used as a prison from at least 1439.

name: Clausentum
text: Your train passes near Bitterne Manor, on the train's {side}, the site of the Roman settlement of Clausentum, the forerunner of Southampton. The manor house was built from its stones.

name: Woolston Floating Bridge
text: Your train passes near where the Woolston Floating Bridge crossed the River Itchen, on the train's {side}: a cable ferry that ran from 1836 until 1977, when the Itchen Bridge opened.

name: Jesus Chapel, Peartree Green
text: Your train passes near Jesus Chapel on Peartree Green, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1620. Its service is said to have set the pattern for later Church of England consecrations.

name: Netley Abbey
text: Your train passes near Netley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1239 for Cistercian monks, who were known for their kindness to travellers. Its ruins later inspired Romantic poets and artists.

name: Royal Victoria Hospital chapel
text: Your train passes near the chapel of the Royal Victoria Hospital, on the train's {side}, a military hospital begun in 1856. Its main building was the longest in the world when finished; all but the chapel and one other building were knocked down in 1966.

name: The Jolly Sailor, Bursledon
text: Your train passes near the Jolly Sailor at Bursledon, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century pub on the River Hamble that you can reach by boat. It was built as a vicarage and has been a pub since 1845.

name: Grace Dieu
text: Your train passes near the wreck of the Grace Dieu in the River Hamble, on the train's {side}: Henry V's flagship, launched in 1418 and twice the size of the Mary Rose. She made only one voyage and burned after being struck by lightning in 1439.

name: Titchfield Abbey
text: Your train passes near Titchfield Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1222. After the abbey was closed in 1537 it became a mansion, later the home of Henry Wriothesley, a patron of Shakespeare.

name: Cams Hall
text: Your train passes near Cams Hall, on the train's {side}, a Palladian mansion of about 1770 overlooking Portsmouth Harbour. Listed as derelict in 1989, it was restored in the 1990s.

name: Wymering Manor
text: Your train passes near Wymering Manor, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in Portsmouth. The manor is first recorded in 1042, when it belonged to King Edward the Confessor.

name: Hilsea Lines
text: Your train passes through the Hilsea Lines, fortifications of the 1700s and 1800s built to guard the way onto Portsea Island, on which most of Portsmouth stands.

name: Fratton Park
text: Your train passes near Fratton Park, on the train's {side}, home of Portsmouth Football Club since 1899. Being on Portsea Island, it is the only professional English football ground not on the mainland of Great Britain.

name: Portsmouth Guildhall
text: Your train passes near Portsmouth Guildhall, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 as the town hall. It was badly damaged by bombing in the Second World War and largely rebuilt in the 1950s.

name: HMS Warrior
text: Your train passes near HMS Warrior, on the train's {side}. Built in 1859 to 1861, she and her sister ship were the first armour-plated, iron-hulled warships. For more than 50 years she served as an oil jetty.

name: Greenford station
text: Your train passes Greenford station. It was the first London Underground station with an escalator up to the platforms, and until 2014 it had the last wooden escalator on the Underground.

name: St Mary's Perivale
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Perivale, on the train's {side}, a church of the 12th or 13th century, once the smallest in Middlesex. Cut off from its parish by the A40, it is now an arts centre.

name: Cuckoo Schools
text: Your train passes near the old Cuckoo Schools, on the train's {side}, opened in 1857 for children of destitute families from London. A working farm educated and fed them until the school closed in 1933.

name: The Drayton Court
text: Your train passes near the Drayton Court, on the train's {side}, opened in 1894 and a hotel until the 1940s. In 1914 Ho Chi Minh, later the leader of Vietnam, worked in its kitchens.

name: Gatwick Racecourse
text: Your train passes near the site of Gatwick Racecourse, on the train's {side}, now part of the airport. The course opened in 1891 beside the railway, and during the First World War it held a stand-in for the Grand National.

name: Tamar Bridge
text: Your train passes the Tamar Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the A38 beside the Royal Albert Bridge. When it opened in 1961 it was the longest suspension bridge in Britain.

name: Severn Beach
text: Your train passes near Severn Beach, on the train's {side}, farmland until the railway came. In the 1920s it became a seaside resort for Bristol, with an open-air pool called the Blue Lagoon, a boating lake and donkey rides.

name: Brislington House
text: Your train passes near Brislington House, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1806 as one of the first purpose-built asylums in England. Its design influenced later asylums and Acts of Parliament.

name: Sexey's Hospital
text: Your train passes near Sexey's Hospital in Bruton, on the train's {side}, almshouses built in about 1630 from the will of Hugh Sexey, an auditor of the Exchequer to James I. People still live there.

name: Swanborough Tump
text: Your train passes near Swanborough Tump, on the train's {side}, a mound where King Aethelred and his brother, the future Alfred the Great, met in 871 on their way to fight the Danes.

name: St James's Church, Trowbridge
text: Your train passes near St James's Church in Trowbridge, on the train's {side}, built in the 1400s. The poet George Crabbe, rector from 1814 to 1832, is buried there.

name: Croome Court
text: Your train passes near the park of Croome Court, on the train's {side}: the first landscape designed by Capability Brown, who also designed the house, for the Earl of Coventry in the 1700s.

name: Priory Cottages, Steventon
text: Your train passes near Priory Cottages at Steventon, on the train's {side}, a manor house of the 1300s that was a grange of the Abbey of Bec in Normandy. A group of women philanthropists, Ferguson's Gang, gave it to the National Trust in 1939.

name: Exeter underground passages
text: Your train passes near Exeter's underground passages, on the train's {side}, built to bring water into the medieval city. The oldest date from the 1200s, and you can take a guided tour.

name: Battle of Pinhoe
text: Your train passes near Pinhoe, on the train's {side}, where the men of Devon and Somerset fought the Danes in 1001. The Danes broke through and burned the village.

name: Cranbrook
text: Your train passes Cranbrook, on the train's {side}, a new town built on what was farmland. Its first houses were lived in from 2012.

name: Whimple
text: Your train passes near Whimple, on the train's {side}, home of Whiteway's cider until 1985. The village is still surrounded by cider apple orchards.

name: Pomeroy Wood
text: Your train passes near Pomeroy Wood, on the train's {side}, where a Roman military site, probably a fort or a marching camp, was found when the A30 was improved in the 1990s. Its garrison seems to have included cavalry.
